primary.thesis: The July 28-29 meeting was over by 2026-08-02, and every listed combination except 'Other' begins with a July pause. My thesis is that the FOMC cuts at least once at the September or October meeting. Three things drive that. Leadership changed after Powell's term as chair ended in May 2026, and the new chair favours easing. The White House is pressing openly for lower rates. And after the easing cycle that ran through late 2025, the Committee keeps trimming once the labour market softens and the one-time price effect of tariffs fades. A long hold through October would need a clear re-acceleration in inflation. A hike would need a sharp inflation shock, which is not in my scenario. So the basket covers every 'pause, then at least one cut' path.

basket.reason: A single cut in September, then a pause in October to watch the data. This is the path when a new chair makes one early cut but still has to win over the rest of the Committee.
Cuts in both September and October. This is the path when payrolls or unemployment worsen over the summer, or when the new leadership pushes a faster pace of easing.
A pause in September, then a first cut in October. This is the path when the Committee waits for one more inflation print, or when dissents slow the new chair, before it moves.

failure_narrative: The basket loses in two ways. The first is a hold at all three meetings (C1). Inflation stays sticky or picks up again: tariff pass-through keeps core goods prices high, oil or energy prices spike, or wage growth stays firm. Growth and payrolls hold up, so regional-bank presidents and governors resist the new chair. The Committee then keeps rates unchanged in September and October, possibly with dissents favouring tighter policy and a statement stressing inflation risk. The second is 'Other' (C5). The July decision was not a pause, or the Fed hikes, or it makes an unusual move such as cutting at every meeting.
hedge_thesis: The primary fails mainly in a world where US inflation and nominal growth run hot enough to override the pressure to ease. In that world, rates are held higher for longer. Short-term and 10-year Treasury yields rise. The dollar strengthens against the euro and yen because the gap between US and foreign rates widens instead of closing. Breakeven inflation rises. Banks earn wider lending margins, while rate-sensitive assets such as homebuilders, mortgage rates and long-duration growth stocks come under pressure. The link is direct. The data that block a September or October cut are the same data that push yields and the dollar up: hot CPI and PCE readings, strong payrolls and high energy prices. So positions in US rates, the dollar and inflation-linked markets pay off in the worlds where the cut basket loses.
